Tensorial Formulation of Backpropagation

The matrix formulation of both feed-foward neural networks and convolutional neural networks (and other networks as well, for example, transformers) is inspired by the linear relationship between the parameters of the network. However, when the dimensions of the space the parameters live in begins to grow, and so do the relationships between parameters, matrices become an inappropriate tool to mathematically describe the model and a rather clumsy tool to describe the backpropogation algorithm, so here, tensors are chosen instead.

1. Feed Forward Neural Networks

We will call a neural network a layered model that produces features of samples in a "linear" way, by using parameters and the sample features at previous layers and then applying a non-linear transform. Define the following:
  • Dataset: D={({xˉi,j}j∈J,vˉi)}i∈I\mathcal{D} = \{(\{\bar{x}^{i,j}\}_{j \in J}, \bar{v}^i)\}_{i \in I}D={({xˉi,j}j∈J​,vˉi)}i∈I​ for some index set III, where xi,j∈Rnx^{i,j} \in \mathbb{R}^nxi,j∈Rn is the jth feature of sample iii and vi∈Rv^i \in \mathbb{R}vi∈R is its label
  • The jjjth feature of the iiith sample produced at hidden layer l−1l-1l−1, feeding into hidden layer lll. (yl)i,j(y_{l})^{i,j}(yl​)i,j
Suppose now we have (yl−1)i,j(y_{l-1})^{i,j}(yl−1​)i,j for every jjj in some index set Vl−1\mathcal{V}_{l-1}Vl−1​. We aim to produce [one of] the next features (yl)i,k(y_{l})^{i,k}(yl​)i,k for the same sample iii; namely feature number k∈Vlk \in \mathcal{V}_lk∈Vl​ not necessarily equal to jjj. The feed-forward neural network (FFN) achieves this in two steps:
  1. We take a set of parameters {(Wl)j,k∈R}j∈Vl−1∪{(bl)k}\{(W_l)^{j,k} \in \mathbb{R}\}_{j \in \mathcal{V}_{l-1}} \cup \{(b_l)^k\}{(Wl​)j,k∈R}j∈Vl−1​​∪{(bl​)k} - we may also call these weights and biases - and multiply each to the respective jjjth feature of the iiith sample at layer l−1l-1l−1, before summing. That is, we produce (zl)i,k=∑j∈Vl−1(yl−1)i,j(Wl)j,k+(bl)k\begin{equation} (z_l)^{i,k} = \sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}_{l-1}}(y_{l-1})^{i,j} (W_l)^{j,k} + (b_l)^k \end{equation}(zl​)i,k=j∈Vl−1​∑​(yl−1​)i,j(Wl​)j,k+(bl​)k​​ a "preimage" of the kkkth feature of the iiith sample at layer lll. Just the preimage thus far, since at step 2...
  2. a smooth, nonlinear transform from C∞(R,R)C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})C∞(R,R) is henceforth applied: (yl)i,k=fl((zl)i,k)\begin{equation} (y_l)^{i,k} = f_l((z_l)^{i,k}) \end{equation}(yl​)i,k=fl​((zl​)i,k)​​ producing the desired feature.

Tensors

It is at this point we will specify important details needed to understand the rest of the article. Firstly, we will use Einstein's Summation Convention (ESC) to simplify sums with a repeated index, signifying the summation of the terms over said index. For example, we can rewrite (1) as (zl)i,k=(yl−1)i,j(Wl)j,k+bk\begin{equation} (z_l)^{i,k} = (y_{l-1})^{i,j} (W_l)^{j,k} + b^k \end{equation}(zl​)i,k=(yl−1​)i,j(Wl​)j,k+bk​​ where the sum is meant to be over jjj, which repeats, and where all terms are zero outside of their domains. This too deserves formalization. Firstly, let's consider (yl)(y_l)(yl​) as a well defined object, namely, a tensor over infinite dimensional vector spaces, but with finite support. Let's clarify, since the (yl)a,b(y_l)^{a,b}(yl​)a,b objects encompass Vl\mathcal{V}_lVl​ features for nnn samples, lets define xˉ=∑i,jxi,jei⊗ej∈RZ⊗RZvˉ=∑iviei∈RZyl=∑i,k(yl)i,kei⊗ek∈RZ⊗RZWl=∑j,k(Wl)j,kej⊗ek∈RZ⊗RZbl=∑i,k(bl)i,kei⊗ek∈RZ⊗RZ\begin{align} \bar{\bf x} &= \sum_{i,j} x^{i,j} e_i \otimes e_j \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}} \otimes \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}} \\ \bar{\bf v} &= \sum_i v^i e_i \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}}\\ y_l &= \sum_{i,k} (y_l)^{i,k} e_i \otimes e_k \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}} \otimes \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}} \\ W_l &= \sum_{j,k} (W_l)^{j,k} e_j \otimes e_k \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}} \otimes \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}} \\ b_l &= \sum_{i,k} (b_l)^{i,k} e_i \otimes e_k \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}} \otimes \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}} \end{align}xˉvˉyl​Wl​bl​​=i,j∑​xi,jei​⊗ej​∈RZ⊗RZ=i∑​viei​∈RZ=i,k∑​(yl​)i,kei​⊗ek​∈RZ⊗RZ=j,k∑​(Wl​)j,kej​⊗ek​∈RZ⊗RZ=i,k∑​(bl​)i,kei​⊗ek​∈RZ⊗RZ​​ where (bl)i,k=(bl)i′,k=(bl)k(b_l)^{i,k} = (b_l)^{i',k} = (b_l)^k(bl​)i,k=(bl​)i′,k=(bl​)k for all i,i′i,i'i,i′.
Throughout the article, V=RZ\mathbb{V} = \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}}V=RZ and V⊗2=V⊗V\mathbb{V}^{\otimes 2} = \mathbb{V} \otimes \mathbb{V}V⊗2=V⊗V so vˉ∈V\bar{\bf v} \in \mathbb{V}vˉ∈V and xˉ,yl,Wl,zl,bl∈V⊗2\bar{\bf x}, y_l,W_l,z_l,b_l \in \mathbb{V}^{\otimes 2}xˉ,yl​,Wl​,zl​,bl​∈V⊗2.
We will also make use of Abstract Index Notation (AIN), which is particularly useful when representing the shape of a tensor. For example, we could write (yl)ab(y_l)^{ab}(yl​)ab to denote that yl∈V⊗Vy_l \in V \otimes Vyl​∈V⊗V, or for a more general example TabcdeT^{ab}{}_{c}{}^{d}{}_{e}Tabc​de​ to denote a tensor T∈V⊗V⊗V∗⊗V⊗V∗T \in V \otimes V \otimes V^* \otimes V \otimes V^*T∈V⊗V⊗V∗⊗V⊗V∗.
We proceed from the tensorized version of (1) (zl)i,kei⊗ek=((yl−1)i,j(Wl)j,k+(bl)i,k)ei⊗ek  ⟹  zl=∑i,j,k(yl−1)i,j(Wl)j,kei⊗ek+∑i,k(bl)i,kei⊗ek∈V⊗V\begin{align} (z_l)^{i,k} e_i \otimes e_k &= ((y_{l-1})^{i,j} (W_l)^{j,k} + (b_l)^{i,k} ) e_i \otimes e_k \\ \implies z_l &= \sum_{i,j,k} (y_{l-1})^{i,j} (W_l)^{j,k} e_i \otimes e_k + \sum_{i,k} (b_l)^{i,k} e_i \otimes e_k \in V \otimes V \end{align}(zl​)i,kei​⊗ek​⟹zl​​=((yl−1​)i,j(Wl​)j,k+(bl​)i,k)ei​⊗ek​=i,j,k∑​(yl−1​)i,j(Wl​)j,kei​⊗ek​+i,k∑​(bl​)i,kei​⊗ek​∈V⊗V​​ We also need to transform the C∞(R,R)C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{R})C∞(R,R) transform into one that acts on tensors, that is one from C∞(V⊗V,V⊗V)C^{\infty}(V \otimes V, V \otimes V )C∞(V⊗V,V⊗V) by defining yl=Fl(zl)=∑i,kfl((zl)i,k)ei⊗ek\begin{equation} y_l = F_l(z_l) = \sum_{i,k} f_l((z_l)^{i,k}) e_i \otimes e_k \end{equation}yl​=Fl​(zl​)=i,k∑​fl​((zl​)i,k)ei​⊗ek​​​

Contraction, Inner Products, Metric Tensors


The issue with (8) is that is kind of useless; we want to speak in a language of tensors and yet are using the coefficients of the layer features and parameters, instead of working with their tensor representations directly. Using basic linear algebra, one realizes that (8) can be formulated as a matrix product, where the inner product is over the space indexed by jjj. Using tensors however, we see (6) as the image of the metric tensor, or, if one of the jjj were lowered, as a contraction. Before jumping in, we need to agree on contraction notation; in (AIN) this is straighforward: if it had been the case that our tensors were of mixed (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) rank, we could write (zl)ac=(yl−1)ab(Wl)bc+(bl)ac\begin{equation} (z_l)^a{}_c = (y_{l-1})^a{}_b (W_l)^b{}_c + (b_l)^a{}_c \end{equation}(zl​)ac​=(yl−1​)ab​(Wl​)bc​+(bl​)ac​​​ However, we actually want to write contraction as a well-formed function, since we will need to derivate later, so lets agree on the convention
Ci1…iϕi1′…iϕ′(T):=contraction over covector and contravector slot ij,ij′ for each jC_{i_1 \ldots i_{\phi}}^{i'_1 \ldots i'_{\phi}}(T) := \text{contraction over covector and contravector slot } i_j, i'_j \text{ for each } jCi1​…iϕ​i1′​…iϕ′​​(T):=contraction over covector and contravector slot ij​,ij′​ for each j
assuming of course TTT is homogenous over the iiith and jjjth slots (i.e they are over the same vector space up-to duality). Rewriting the equation for our (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) tensors: zl=C23(yl⊗Wl)+bl\begin{equation} z_l = C^3_2(y_l \otimes W_l) + b_l \end{equation}zl​=C23​(yl​⊗Wl​)+bl​​​
Unfortunately our tensors arent of rank (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and the shared index across yl−1,Wly_{l-1}, W_lyl−1​,Wl​ is across (V,V)(V, V)(V,V) not (V∗,V)(V^*, V)(V∗,V), so the operation we're looking for is the inner-product, or, contraction against a metric tensor. We should talk briefly about the metric tensor gabg_{ab}gab​ and the inverse metric tensor gab{g}^{ab}gab. VVV has the canonical orthonormal basis, and is endowed with the canonical inner product. For VVV, the basis is {ei}\{e_i\}{ei​} and the inner product is given by ⟨ei,ej⟩=δij\langle e_i, e_j \rangle = \delta_{ij}⟨ei​,ej​⟩=δij​. For the dual space V∗V^*V∗, the basis is {ei}\{e^i\}{ei} with inner product ⟨ei,ej⟩=δij\langle e^i, e^j \rangle = \delta_{ij}⟨ei,ej⟩=δij​. The metric tensors are then given by agreement with the inner products gab=gi,jei⊗ej=δijei⊗ejgab=gi,jei⊗ej=δijei⊗ej\begin{align} g_{ab} = g_{i,j} e^i \otimes e^j = \delta_{ij} e^i \otimes e^j \\ {g}^{ab} = g^{i,j} e_i \otimes e_j = \delta_{ij} e_i \otimes e_j \end{align}gab​=gi,j​ei⊗ej=δij​ei⊗ejgab=gi,jei​⊗ej​=δij​ei​⊗ej​​​ Typically we would fully contract either tensor against the product of two input tensors, however we are going to need to denote partially contracting against the metric tensor. Thus let us generalize the previously mentioned metrics using maps
Gi1…iϕ,i1′…iϕ′j1…jψ,j1′…jψ′(A,B)G_{i_1 \ldots i_{\phi}, i'_1 \ldots i'_{\phi}}^{j_1 \ldots j_{\psi}, j'_1 \ldots j'_{\psi}}(A,B)Gi1​…iϕ​,i1′​…iϕ′​j1​…jψ​,j1′​…jψ′​​(A,B) =Ca1…aϕ,b1…bϕ,j1…jψ,j1′…jψ′i1…iϕ,i1′…iϕ′,c1…cψ,d1…dψ(⨂m≤ϕgambm⨂n≤ψgcndn⊗A⊗B)= C_{a_1 \ldots a_{\phi}, b_1 \ldots b_{\phi}, j_1 \ldots j_{\psi}, j'_1 \ldots j'_{\psi}}^{i_1 \ldots i_{\phi}, i'_1 \ldots i'_{\phi},c_1 \ldots c_{\psi}, d_1 \ldots d_{\psi}}(\bigotimes_{m\leq \phi} g_{a_mb_m} \bigotimes_{n \leq \psi} g^{c_nd_n} \otimes A \otimes B)=Ca1​…aϕ​,b1​…bϕ​,j1​…jψ​,j1′​…jψ′​i1​…iϕ​,i1′​…iϕ′​,c1​…cψ​,d1​…dψ​​(m≤ϕ⨂​gam​bm​​n≤ψ⨂​gcn​dn​⊗A⊗B) =gi1i1′…giϕiϕ′gj1j1′…gjψjψ′AB= g_{i_1i'_1}\ldots g_{i_{\phi}i'_{\phi}} g^{j_1j'_1} \ldots g^{j_{\psi}j'_{\psi}}AB=gi1​i1′​​…giϕ​iϕ′​​gj1​j1′​…gjψ​jψ′​AB =contraction of A⊗B against each gab over contravariant slots ip,ip′= \text{contraction of } A \otimes B \text{ against each } g_{ab} \text{ over contravariant slots } i_p, i'_p=contraction of A⊗B against each gab​ over contravariant slots ip​,ip′​ and gab over covariant slots jq,jq′ of A,B resp. \text{and } g^{ab} \text{ over covariant slots } j_q, j'_q \text{ of } A,B \text{ resp. }and gab over covariant slots jq​,jq′​ of A,B resp. 
Now we can find a suitable tensorial representation for (8) in terms of tensors, not coefficients.
zl=(yl−1)i,j(Wl)j,kei⊗ek+(bl)i,kei⊗ek=Gb,c((yl−1)ab,(Wl)cd)+(bl)adz_l = (y_{l-1})^{i,j}(W_l)^{j,k}e_i \otimes e_k + (b_l)^{i,k} e_i \otimes e_k= G_{b,c}((y_{l-1})^{ab}, (W_l)^{cd}) + (b_l)^{ad}zl​=(yl−1​)i,j(Wl​)j,kei​⊗ek​+(bl​)i,kei​⊗ek​=Gb,c​((yl−1​)ab,(Wl​)cd)+(bl​)ad

The Model

We now formalize the FNN model F\mathcal{F}F completely.

  • We will call a layer l=1...Ll=1...Ll=1...L the function yl−1↦Ll(yl−1;Wl,bl)=Γl(yl−1,Wl,bl)y_{l-1} \mapsto \mathcal{L}_l(y_{l-1} ; W_l, b_l) = \Gamma_l(y_{l-1}, W_l, b_l)yl−1​↦Ll​(yl−1​;Wl​,bl​)=Γl​(yl−1​,Wl​,bl​) where Γl(S,T,U)=Fl(gbcSabTcd+U)\begin{equation} \Gamma_{l}(S, T, U) = F_l(g_{bc}S^{ab}T^{cd}+ U) \end{equation}Γl​(S,T,U)=Fl​(gbc​SabTcd+U)​​ We will call the neuron kkk at layer lll the function yl−1↦Nl,k(yl−1;Wl,bl)=γl,k(yl−1,Wl,bl)y_{l-1} \mapsto \mathcal{N}_{l,k}(y_{l-1} ; W_l, b_l) = \gamma_{l,k}(y_{l-1}, W_l, b_l)yl−1​↦Nl,k​(yl−1​;Wl​,bl​)=γl,k​(yl−1​,Wl​,bl​) where γl,k(S,T,U)=Fl(gbcSab(Tjkej⊗ek)cd+Ui,kei⊗ek)\gamma_{l,k}(S, T, U) = F_l(g_{bc}S^{ab}(T^{jk} e_j \otimes e_k)^{cd}+U^{i,k}e_i \otimes e_k)γl,k​(S,T,U)=Fl​(gbc​Sab(Tjkej​⊗ek​)cd+Ui,kei​⊗ek​)=Γl(S,Tjkej⊗ek,Ui,kei⊗ek)= \Gamma_l(S, T^{jk} e_j \otimes e_k, U^{i,k}e_i \otimes e_k)=Γl​(S,Tjkej​⊗ek​,Ui,kei​⊗ek​) Note that ∑kγl,k(S,T,U)=Γl(S,T,U)\sum_k \gamma_{l,k}(S, T, U) = \Gamma_l(S, T, U)k∑​γl,k​(S,T,U)=Γl​(S,T,U) that is, a layer is a sum of neurons.
  • First we start with the input layer , L0\mathcal{L}_0L0​. We define y0:=xy_0 := xy0​:=x for any sample x∈V⊗Vx \in V \otimes Vx∈V⊗V and define L0\mathcal{L}_0L0​ by x↦y0x \mapsto y_0x↦y0​, so L0\mathcal{L}_0L0​ is the identity. It's not strictly a computational layer like defined earlier, however some folks like to speak of an input layer, which refers to this.
  • The hidden layers are {Ll}l=1…L\{\mathcal{L}_l\}_{ l=1\dots L}{Ll​}l=1…L​

  • The model F\mathcal{F}F is defined by F(x;θ)=LL+1(⋅;WL+1,bL+1)∘…∘L1(⋅;W1,b1)∘L0(x)\mathcal{F}(x ; \theta) = \mathcal{L}_{L+1}(\cdot ; W_{L+1},b_{L+1}) \circ \ldots \circ \mathcal{L}_{1}(\cdot ; W_{1}, b_1) \circ \mathcal{L_0} (x)F(x;θ)=LL+1​(⋅;WL+1​,bL+1​)∘…∘L1​(⋅;W1​,b1​)∘L0​(x) where θ=W1,b1…WL+1,bL+1\theta = W_1,b_1 \ldots W_{L+1},b_{L+1}θ=W1​,b1​…WL+1​,bL+1​ are the parameters of the model.

Loss, Empirical Risk

We have so far the ability to compute the output of our parameterized model yL+1=F(x;θ)y_{L+1} = \mathcal{F}(x;\theta)yL+1​=F(x;θ).

Let X,YX,YX,Y be the random variables for input features and labels, over the spaces X=V,Y=R\mathcal{X} = \mathbb{V}, \mathcal{Y} = \mathbb{R}X=V,Y=R. Let X,Y∼P(X,Y)X,Y \sim \mathcal{P}(X,Y)X,Y∼P(X,Y) with pdf pX,Y(x,y)p_{X,Y}(x,y)pX,Y​(x,y). Let Xi,YiX_i,Y_iXi​,Yi​ be the ith feature and label random variables, and assume Xi,Yi∼i.i.dP(X,Y)X_i, Y_i \sim_{i.i.d} \mathcal{P}(X,Y)Xi​,Yi​∼i.i.d​P(X,Y) Define a loss function R×V→R:\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{V} \to \mathbb{R}:R×V→R: w,w^↦Δ(w,w^)w, \hat{w} \mapsto \Delta(w, \hat{w})w,w^↦Δ(w,w^) Define T[i]=∑αTi,αei⊗eαT⟩i⟨=∑αTi,αeαT⟨i⟩=∑αTαei⊗eα=ei⊗T\begin{align*} T^{[i]} &= \sum_{\alpha} T^{i,\alpha} e_i \otimes e_{\alpha} \\ T^{\rangle i \langle} &= \sum_{\alpha} T^{i,\alpha} e_{\alpha} \\ T^{\langle i \rangle}& = \sum_{\alpha} T^{\alpha} e_i \otimes e_{\alpha} = e_i \otimes T \end{align*}T[i]T⟩i⟨T⟨i⟩​=α∑​Ti,αei​⊗eα​=α∑​Ti,αeα​=α∑​Tαei​⊗eα​=ei​⊗T​ For a batch model hhh (one defined over V⊗2\mathbb{V}^{\otimes 2}V⊗2 like ours), the loss at a point (x,y)∈V×R(x,y) \in \mathbb{V} \times \mathbb{R}(x,y)∈V×R is l(x,y,h)=Δ(y,h(x⟨μ⟩)⟩μ⟨)l(x, y,h) = \Delta(y, h(x^{\langle \mu \rangle})^{\rangle \mu \langle})l(x,y,h)=Δ(y,h(x⟨μ⟩)⟩μ⟨) The risk is the expected value of the loss over X×YX \times YX×Y R(h)=EX,Y(l(x,y,h))=∫l(x,y,h)pX,Y(x,y)dxdyR(h) = \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}(l(x,y,h)) = \int l(x,y,h) p_{X,Y}(x,y) dxdyR(h)=EX,Y​(l(x,y,h))=∫l(x,y,h)pX,Y​(x,y)dxdy which is intractable, so the empirical risk over a sample d=(x,y)\bm{d}=( \bm{x}, \bm{y})d=(x,y) is used instead, which, as data size grows, converges to the risk by the LLN: R^(d,h)=1I∑il(x⟩i⟨,yi,h)=1I∑il(x⟩i⟨,y⟩i⟨,h)→EX,Y(l(x,y,h))\begin{equation} \hat{R}(\bm{d}, h) = \frac{1}{I}\sum_i l({\bf x}^{\rangle i \langle},y^i,h) = \frac{1}{I}\sum_i l(\bm{x}^{\rangle i \langle},\bm{y}^{\rangle i \langle},h) \to \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}(l(x,y,h)) \end{equation}R^(d,h)=I1​i∑​l(x⟩i⟨,yi,h)=I1​i∑​l(x⟩i⟨,y⟩i⟨,h)→EX,Y​(l(x,y,h))​​as I→∞I\to\inftyI→∞. Empirical Risk Minimization chooses a model space, in this case, H={F(⋅;θ)}θ\mathcal{H} = \{\mathcal{F}(\cdot;\theta) \}_{\theta}H={F(⋅;θ)}θ​ and finds arg min⁡h∈HR^(d,h)=F(⋅;θ∗),θ∗=arg min⁡θR^(d,F(⋅;θ))\argmin_{h \in \mathcal{H}}\hat{R}(\bm{d}, h) = \mathcal{F}(\cdot;\theta^*), \theta^* = \argmin_{\theta}\hat{R}({\bm d}, \mathcal{F}(\cdot ; \theta))h∈Hargmin​R^(d,h)=F(⋅;θ∗),θ∗=θargmin​R^(d,F(⋅;θ)) so given our sample dˉ=(xˉ,vˉ)\bar{\bm{d}} = (\bar{\bm{x}}, \bar{\bm{v}})dˉ=(xˉ,vˉ) we find arg min⁡θR^(dˉ,F(⋅;θ))=arg min⁡θ1I∑il(xˉ⟩i⟨,vˉi,F(⋅;θ))=arg min⁡θ1I∑iΔ(vˉi,F(xˉ⟩i⟨⟨i⟩;θ)⟩i⟨)=arg min⁡θ1I∑iΔ(vˉi,F(xˉ[i];θ)⟩i⟨)\argmin_{\theta} \hat{R}(\bar{\bm{d}}, \mathcal{F}(\cdot ; \theta)) = \argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{I}\sum_i l(\bar{\bf x}^{\rangle i \langle},\bar{v}^i, \mathcal{F}(\cdot; \theta)) \\ = \argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{I}\sum_i \Delta(\bar{v}^i, \mathcal{F}(\bar{\bf x}^{\rangle i \langle \langle i \rangle}; \theta)^{\rangle i \langle }) = \argmin_{\theta}\frac{1}{I}\sum_i\Delta(\bar{v}^i, \mathcal{F}(\bar{\bf x}^{[i]} ; \theta)^{\rangle i \langle} )θargmin​R^(dˉ,F(⋅;θ))=θargmin​I1​i∑​l(xˉ⟩i⟨,vˉi,F(⋅;θ))=θargmin​I1​i∑​Δ(vˉi,F(xˉ⟩i⟨⟨i⟩;θ)⟩i⟨)=θargmin​I1​i∑​Δ(vˉi,F(xˉ[i];θ)⟩i⟨)

Loss Function, Activation Functions

We will need a way to choose the loss function Δ\DeltaΔ. While we could make an arbitrary choice, we could also use Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) to derive it. Let T(⋅,θ)=ΓL+1(⋅;θL+1)∘...∘L0Ul(⋅,θ)=ΓL+1(⋅;θL+1)∘FL∘...∘Fl+1∘Γl+1(⋅;θl+1)\begin{align*} T(\cdot, \theta) &= \Gamma_{L+1}(\cdot; \theta_{L+1}) \circ ... \circ \mathcal{L}_0 \\ U_l(\cdot, \theta) &= \Gamma_{L+1}(\cdot; \theta_{L+1}) \circ F_{L} \circ ... \circ F_{l+1} \circ \Gamma_{l+1}(\cdot; \theta_{l+1}) \end{align*}T(⋅,θ)Ul​(⋅,θ)​=ΓL+1​(⋅;θL+1​)∘...∘L0​=ΓL+1​(⋅;θL+1​)∘FL​∘...∘Fl+1​∘Γl+1​(⋅;θl+1​)​ for l=L…1l=L\ldots 1l=L…1. T(xˉ,θ)=(Ul(⋅,θ)∘Fl∘Γl(⋅;θl)∘…∘L0)(xˉ)  ⟹  ∂θlT(xˉ,θ)=∂1Ul(yl,θ)∘DFl(zl)∘∂2Γl(yl−1;θl)\begin{align*} T(\bar{\bf x}, \theta) &= \left( U_l(\cdot, \theta) \circ F_l \circ \Gamma_l(\cdot; \theta_l) \circ \ldots \circ \mathcal{L}_0 \right)(\bar{\bf x}) \\ \implies \partial_{\theta_l} T(\bar{\bf x}, \theta) &= \partial_{1} U_l({\bf y}_l, \theta) \circ DF_l({\bf z}_l) \circ \partial_{2}\Gamma_l({\bf y}_{l-1}; \theta_l) \\ \end{align*}T(xˉ,θ)⟹∂θl​​T(xˉ,θ)​=(Ul​(⋅,θ)∘Fl​∘Γl​(⋅;θl​)∘…∘L0​)(xˉ)=∂1​Ul​(yl​,θ)∘DFl​(zl​)∘∂2​Γl​(yl−1​;θl​)​ where Ul(⋅,θ)={Ul+1(⋅,θ)∘Fl+1∘Γl+1(⋅;θl+1)l=1…L−1ΓL+1(⋅;θL+1)l=L  ⟹  ∂1Ul(yl,θ)={∂1Ul+1(yl+1,θ)∘DFl+1(zl+1)∘∂1Γl+1(yl,θ)l=1…L−1∂1ΓL+1(yL;θL+1)l=L\begin{align*} U_{l}(\cdot, \theta) &= \begin{cases} U_{l+1}(\cdot, \theta) \circ F_{l+1} \circ \Gamma_{l+1}(\cdot; \theta_{l+1}) & l=1\ldots L-1\\ \Gamma_{L+1}(\cdot; \theta_{L+1}) & l=L \end{cases} \\ \implies \partial_{1} U_l({\bf y}_l, \theta) &= \begin{cases} \partial_{1} U_{l+1}({\bf y}_{l+1}, \theta) \circ DF_{l+1}({\bf z}_{l+1}) \circ \partial_1 \Gamma_{l+1}({\bf y}_l, \theta) & l=1\ldots L-1 \\ \partial_1 \Gamma_{L+1}({\bf y}_{L}; \theta_{L+1}) & l = L \end{cases} \end{align*}Ul​(⋅,θ)⟹∂1​Ul​(yl​,θ)​={Ul+1​(⋅,θ)∘Fl+1​∘Γl+1​(⋅;θl+1​)ΓL+1​(⋅;θL+1​)​l=1…L−1l=L​={∂1​Ul+1​(yl+1​,θ)∘DFl+1​(zl+1​)∘∂1​Γl+1​(yl​,θ)∂1​ΓL+1​(yL​;θL+1​)​l=1…L−1l=L​​ So the recursion is well posed.
